segments.name: The Marmaritae, and the Man with the Dog's Head

stops.name: Marmarica, birth among the dog-headed tribe
stops.date_confidence: legendary; the earliest Greek Passion is 5th-6th century and no contemporary record of any 3rd-century Christopher exists
stops.campa: West of Egypt, in the scrub the Romans call Marmarica, a son is born among the Marmaritae, a tribe the Greek Passion describes as giants, eaters of men, and dog-headed. He has the head of a dog and the speech of a dog. His people give him no name that survives; the Greek text calls him Adokimos and the Latin Reprobus, the rejected one, the one who did not pass. He grows to twelve cubits. Nothing in the province records his birth, and the nearest fixed point inside his tribe's country is the harbour of Paraetonium.
suggested_refs: The Marmaric coast between Paraetonium (Mersa Matruh) and Cyrenaica, country of the Marmaritae
sources: Early Greek Passion of St. Christopher (BHG 309-310c)
Orthodox Arts Journal, 'Understanding The Dog-Headed Icon of St. Christopher'
Wikipedia, 'Saint Christopher'

stops.name: Antioch, conscription into the numerus Marmaritarum
stops.date_confidence: scholarly reconstruction: Woods (1999) dates the Marmaric campaign to late 301 or early 302 and places the unit in or near Antioch; no primary text names the garrison
stops.campa: Diocletian's army sweeps the Marmaric frontier in the winter, and the captives are not killed but enrolled. Reprobus is pressed into an auxiliary unit named for his own tribe, the numerus Marmaritarum, and marched east to garrison duty in Syria, in or near Antioch. He wears Roman kit and answers Roman orders in a mouth that cannot shape Roman words. David Woods reads the dog's head as the army's shorthand for a man brought in from the edge of the world; the Passion reads it as a fact of his body, and does not explain it.
suggested_refs: Antioch on the Orontes and its Diocletianic garrison quarter
sources: David Woods, 'The Origin of the Cult of St. Christopher' (University College Cork, 1999)
Orthodox Arts Journal, 'Understanding The Dog-Headed Icon of St. Christopher'

stops.name: Antioch, the baptism and the gift of speech
stops.date_confidence: no date given in the sources; placed after the conscription on narrative order alone
stops.campa: In the Eastern tradition he is baptized at Antioch, and the water changes him. From the font he goes out to preach in Lycia and in Samos, and the tongue that could only bark now argues scripture in the market. This strand has no river, no ferry, and no child in it: there is no giant ferryman anywhere in the Eastern life, only a soldier out of a monstrous tribe who is washed at the font and given a name. The Western legend that Genoa will fix in the thirteenth century contradicts it point for point, and no source reconciles the two.
suggested_refs: The baptistery quarter of late-Roman Antioch (Antakya)
sources: OMNES / Omnesmag, 'St. Christopher of Lycia, and martyrs of Syria and Vietnam'
Orthodox Church in America, Lives of the Saints, May 9

stops.name: Egypt, the Coptic Acts of Bartholomew
stops.date_confidence: text dated 4th-5th century; the pin is the Egyptian national centroid, since the text names no site
stops.campa: In Egypt, in a Coptic book of the acts of the apostle Bartholomew, a dog-headed cannibal out of the cynocephalic country is taken by the apostles and converted. He calls himself Bewitched, and the Damned. An angel comes to him, gives him human speech, and names him Christian. He is not yet Christopher and the book does not say where any of it happens. This is where the legend's root is usually placed, four or five centuries before the Golden Legend. The figure at that root has been given speech and a faith, and no name that anyone would recognise.
suggested_refs: The Coptic Acts of Bartholomew, in the Egyptian apocryphal apostolic cycle
sources: Wikipedia, 'Saint Christopher', citing the Coptic hagiographic tradition

segments.name: The Greatest King in the World

stops.name: Lycia, the hall of the greatest king
stops.date_confidence: legendary; the episode is Western and appears first in the Legenda Aurea tradition, c. 1260, with no site named
stops.campa: A giant twelve cubits high walks into the hall of the greatest king he can find and offers his service on one condition: he will serve nobody greater. He serves well. Then a minstrel sings and the word devil falls in the song, and the king crosses himself. The giant asks why. The king will not say. The giant presses until he has it, that the sign is a guard against the devil, whom the king fears. He takes his leave the same hour. The Legend names neither the king nor his country; the pin is Lycia, where the story ends up.
stops.quote: Doubtest thou the devil that he hurt thee not? Then is the devil more mighty and greater than thou art. I am then deceived of my hope and purpose, for I had supposed I had found the most mighty and the most greatest Lord of the world, but I commend thee to God, for I will go seek him for to be my Lord, and I his servant.
stops.quote_source: The Golden Legend, Caxton trans. (1483), Temple Classics ed., 'The Right Great King'
suggested_refs: The unnamed royal hall of the Legenda Aurea, conventionally set in the Lycian interior
sources: Jacobus de Voragine, Legenda Aurea (c. 1260), Caxton trans. 1483
EBSCO Research Starters, 'Saint Christopher'

stops.name: The road, the knight cruel and horrible
stops.date_confidence: legendary; Western episode, no site named
stops.campa: On the road he meets a company of riders led by a knight cruel and horrible of countenance, who asks him where he is going. The giant answers that he goes to seek the devil, to be his master, and the knight says that he is the devil himself. They ride together. At a crossroads there stands a cross, and the devil turns off it and takes the party the long way round through the waste. The giant asks why, and gets nothing, and threatens to leave, and then gets his answer.
stops.quote: There was a man called Christ which was hanged on the cross, and when I see his sign I am sore afraid, and flee from it wheresoever I see it.
stops.quote_source: The Golden Legend, Caxton trans. (1483), Temple Classics ed., 'The Knight Cruel and Horrible'
suggested_refs: The wayside cross at the crossroads, the Legend's turning point
sources: Jacobus de Voragine, Legenda Aurea, Caxton trans. 1483
Catholic Online, 'St. Christopher'

stops.name: Xanthos valley, the hermit's cell above the ford
stops.date_confidence: legendary; the Legenda Aurea names no river, and the pin is a regional anchor in the Xanthos valley of Lycia, not an attested site
stops.campa: He comes to a hermit who keeps a cell by a river, and asks how a man may serve Christ. Fast, says the hermit. The giant says he cannot fast; fasting takes his strength, and his strength is the whole of what he has. Pray, says the hermit. The giant says he does not know how. So the hermit shows him the ford, where the water runs high and travellers drown in the crossing, and tells him to stand in it and carry over whoever comes. The work asks for a body twelve cubits high and asks nothing else of him.
stops.quote: Certes, this service may I well do, and I promise to him for to do it.
stops.quote_source: The Golden Legend, Caxton trans. (1483), Temple Classics ed., 'The Hermit'
suggested_refs: The Xanthos (Esen Cayi) valley below the city of Xanthos, regional anchor for the unnamed river
sources: Jacobus de Voragine, Legenda Aurea, Caxton trans. 1483
EBSCO Research Starters, 'Saint Christopher'

stops.name: The ford, the child and the weight of the world
stops.date_confidence: legendary; the central Western episode, absent from the entire Eastern Greek Passion tradition
stops.campa: He plants a pole in the riverbed for a staff and works the ford by day and by night. One night a child calls from the bank, three times, and on the third call he wades out and lifts the child onto his shoulders. Midstream the water rises and the child grows heavy, and heavier, until the giant is bowed under a weight no man carries. He fights the current to the far bank and sets the child down. The atlas follows this same child to another river, the Jordan at Qasr el-Yahud, where he is baptized as a grown man.
stops.quote: Child, thou hast put me in great peril; thou weighest almost as I had all the world upon me, I might bear no greater burden.
stops.quote_source: The Golden Legend, Caxton trans. (1483), Temple Classics ed., 'Of St. Christopher'
suggested_refs: The unnamed ford of the Legenda Aurea, the crossing that gives the saint his name
sources: Jacobus de Voragine, Legenda Aurea, Caxton trans. 1483
Orthodox Church in America, Lives of the Saints, May 9

stops.name: The far bank, the staff in flower and the new name
stops.date_confidence: legendary; Western episode only
stops.campa: The child tells him what he has carried, and is gone. The giant drives his staff into the earth beside the hermit's cell, and overnight the dead pole puts out leaves and dates, which is the proof. From this crossing he takes the name he keeps: Christopher, the Christ-bearer, over Reprobus, the rejected. The Eastern Passion, older than this Western telling by seven hundred years, knows nothing of a river, a child, or a staff, and gives him the name at the font in Antioch instead.
stops.quote: Christopher, marvel thee nothing, for thou hast not only borne all the world upon thee, but thou hast borne him that created and made all the world, upon thy shoulders. I am Jesu Christ the king, to whom thou servest in this work.
stops.quote_source: The Golden Legend, Caxton trans. (1483), Temple Classics ed., 'Of St. Christopher'
suggested_refs: The flowering staff, standard attribute of Christopher in Western painting
sources: Jacobus de Voragine, Legenda Aurea, Caxton trans. 1483
Orthodox Church in America, Lives of the Saints, May 9

segments.name: Lycia: the Preaching and the Passion

stops.name: Myra, preaching in a city the Legend will not name
stops.date_confidence: traditional; Myra is a regional anchor for Roman Lycia, no town is specified in the sources
stops.campa: He comes into Lycia, where he can neither speak the language nor be understood, and prays for speech. He preaches in the marketplace of a city whose name the Legend declines to give. The judges have him struck in the face, and he answers that were he not a Christian he would avenge the blow. The preface that Caxton's Legend attributes to Ambrose credits him with forty-eight thousand souls called out of the error of the pagans. Myra is the chief city of Roman Lycia and stands here for a preaching-place the sources refuse to fix.
stops.quote: If I were not Christian I should avenge mine injury.
stops.quote_source: The Golden Legend, Caxton trans. (1483), Temple Classics ed., 'He Converts Eight Thousand in Lycia'
suggested_refs: Myra (Demre), metropolis of Roman Lycia
sources: Jacobus de Voragine, Legenda Aurea, Caxton trans. 1483
Martyrologium Hieronymianum
Orthodox Church in America, Lives of the Saints, May 9

stops.name: Samos, the island that may not be an island
stops.date_confidence: contradiction unresolved: the sources say Lycia and Samos without specifying which Samos; the pin sits on the Aegean island, the commoner assumption
stops.campa: The Eastern lives send him from Lycia on to Samos. Which Samos, no source will say. Readers who take it for the Aegean island must send a Lycia-bound giant out on a sea crossing that fits nothing else in the narrative. Readers who take it for a smaller town of the same name on the Lycian coast have no town to point at. The pin sits on the island, with the doubt left standing where the sources leave it. The Western Legend has no Samos in it at all, and no sea.
suggested_refs: The island of Samos, and the unlocated Lycian Samos proposed against it
sources: OMNES / Omnesmag, 'St. Christopher of Lycia'
Orthodox Church in America, Lives of the Saints, May 9

stops.name: Lycia, before King Dagnus
stops.date_confidence: legendary; neither Dagnus nor Dagon is attested outside hagiography, and no court site is locatable
stops.campa: The king of Lycia has him brought in. In the Golden Legend the king is Dagnus; in the Eastern lives he is Dagon, acting on the emperor Decius's orders; no Roman record knows either man. The king offers gifts and honours for one sacrifice to the gods, and torments for a refusal, and remarks that a man raised among wild beasts can speak only wild language and words unknown to men. Christopher answers first with his two names, and then with a pun on the king's.
stops.quote: Tofore or I was baptized I was named Reprobus, and after, I am Christopher; tofore baptism, a Canaanite, now, a Christian man.
stops.quote_source: The Golden Legend, Caxton trans. (1483), Temple Classics ed., 'St. Christopher before the King of Lycia'
suggested_refs: The court of the unlocated King Dagnus of Lycia
sources: Jacobus de Voragine, Legenda Aurea, Caxton trans. 1483
Orthodox Church in America, Lives of the Saints, May 9
Omnesmag, 'St. Christopher of Lycia'

stops.name: Lycia, the prison and the two women
stops.date_confidence: legendary; the Orthodox Life for 9 May gives the year 250, the Golden Legend gives no year
stops.campa: Two women are sent into the cell to break him, Callinika and Aquilina, on the king's orders. They are to seduce him out of his faith. They come out of the cell Christian. They pull down the idols they were raised to serve, and they are executed for it before he is, while the man they were sent to corrupt is still alive in his cell. The Orthodox Life for the ninth of May carries both names and gives the year as 250. The Golden Legend keeps the episode and drops the dating.
suggested_refs: The prison of the Lycian court, unlocated in every source
sources: Orthodox Church in America, Lives of the Saints, May 9
Wikipedia, 'Saint Christopher', citing BHG 309-310c

stops.name: Lycia, the iron seat, the fire and the forty archers
stops.date_confidence: legendary
stops.campa: They heat an iron seat under him and the fire does him no harm. They shut him in a chamber of red-hot metal and he is not burned. They bring forty archers, and the arrows loosed at him hang in the air on every side and will not touch him. One arrow turns in the air and takes the king in the eye. Christopher tells him to wait for the morning, when he will be dead, and to temper clay with the blood at his neck and lay it on the eye. The king listens to the man he is about to kill.
stops.quote: Tyrant, I shall die to-morn, make a little clay, with my blood tempered, and anoint therewith thine eye, and thou shalt receive health.
stops.quote_source: The Golden Legend, Caxton trans. (1483), Temple Classics ed., 'The Forty Archers'
suggested_refs: The place of torments, unnamed in the Passio and in the Legend alike
sources: Jacobus de Voragine, Legenda Aurea, Caxton trans. 1483
OrthodoxWiki, 'Christopher of Lycia'
Orthodox Church in America, Lives of the Saints, May 9

stops.name: Lycia, the beheading and the healed eye
stops.date_confidence: traditional; commemorated 25 July in the West and 9 May in the East, with no contemporary record of the execution
stops.campa: The sword takes his head off. The king comes down to the body, mixes earth with what runs from the neck, lays the clay on his blind eye, and speaks the name of the God he has spent the day trying to kill. The sight comes back. He is baptized. In this atlas Catherine of Alexandria goes to the same sword some sixty years later, and the account of her beheading names Christopher's neck beside her own, because what ran from both, in that tradition, was white as milk. The Golden Legend says blood, and mixes it with clay.
stops.quote: In the name of God and of St. Christopher!
stops.quote_source: The Golden Legend, Caxton trans. (1483), Temple Classics ed., 'The Beheading' (King Dagnus anointing his eye)
suggested_refs: The site of the martyrdom in Lycia, unfixed in every source
sources: Jacobus de Voragine, Legenda Aurea, Caxton trans. 1483
Martyrologium Hieronymianum
catherine_alexandria.journey.json, stop 'Alexandria, the beheading, and the milk'

stops.name: Antioch, the other city that claims the martyrdom
stops.date_confidence: contradiction flagged: sources split between Decius (249-251) and Diocletian (284-305), and between Lycia and Antioch; neither pair is resolved
stops.campa: Another line of the Passion puts the trial and the beheading at Antioch in Syria, not in Lycia at all, and some Latin redactions move the persecutor from Decius to Diocletian, which shifts the martyrdom half a century later and into another reign. The Hieronymian Martyrology, the earliest Western witness, holds to Decius. Margaret of Antioch, who travels in this atlas, dies in the Diocletianic persecution in this same city and shares his chapter-sequence in the Golden Legend. Nothing reconciles the two cities or the two emperors.
suggested_refs: Antioch on the Orontes, rival martyrdom site against Lycia
sources: Martyrologium Hieronymianum
Wikipedia, 'Saint Christopher'
margarita_pelagia.journey.json, 'The Dragon: Margaret of Antioch' arc

segments.name: The Cult, the Text and the Question of the Soul

stops.name: Hippo Regius, Augustine rules on the monstrous races
stops.date_confidence: attested: De Civitate Dei completed c. 426
stops.campa: In Hippo Regius, writing the City of God, Augustine takes up the monstrous races of the geographers: the sciopods, the men with faces in their chests, the dog-headed. He does not deny that they exist. He rules instead that whatever is born of man descends from the one first man, and that no Christian may doubt it. The ruling is made for the margins of maps, with no saint anywhere in view. Four hundred years later it is the text the Franks reach for when they need to know whether Christopher's people have souls.
suggested_refs: The basilica and see of Hippo Regius (Annaba), where the City of God was completed
sources: Augustine, De Civitate Dei, book XVI
JSTOR Daily, 'Christopher the Dog-Headed Saint'

stops.name: Chalcedon, the martyrium consecrated
stops.date_confidence: attested by the consecration record; the earliest firm evidence of an established cult
stops.campa: Across the water from Constantinople, at Chalcedon, a martyrium raised over the name of Christopher is consecrated on the twenty-second of September. This is the first hard evidence that anyone anywhere is keeping his cult: a building, a date, a record in a register. Two hundred years lie between the martyrdom the legend gives him and this stone, and nothing whatever fills them. The council that gave Chalcedon its name had met in this same suburb the year before, on the other side of the strait from the capital.
suggested_refs: The martyrium of St Christopher at Chalcedon (Kadikoy)
sources: Wikipedia, 'Saint Christopher', citing the martyrium consecration record

stops.name: Vinica, the terracotta with the muzzle
stops.date_confidence: attested to the 5th-6th century by the excavated plaque group; no closer date
stops.campa: At Vinica in the Bregalnica valley, a hill fort yields a hoard of fired terracotta plaques, and on one of them a soldier saint stands with the head of a dog. It is the oldest surviving picture of him with the muzzle. Scholars set it beside the jackal-headed Hermanubis of Greco-Egyptian art and argue over the descent. The plaque and the Greek Passion that calls his tribe dog-headed are close enough in date that neither can be shown to follow the other. Which of the two came first is not recoverable from anything now surviving.
suggested_refs: The Vinica Kale terracotta icon collection, North Macedonia
sources: Wikipedia, 'Saint Christopher', citing the Vinica terracotta icons

stops.name: Constantinople, the Greek Passion written down
stops.date_confidence: probably 6th century; Wikipedia dates BHG 309-310c to possibly the 5th century or later, so the century is a scholarly estimate
stops.campa: In the Greek-speaking East a Passion of Saint Christopher is written down, probably in the sixth century, and it becomes the trunk from which the rest grows: the Marmaritae, the cannibal tribe, the dog's head, the conscription, the two women, the arrows, the eye. The manuscripts are catalogued as BHG 309 to 310c, and the key Greek codices sit today among the Vatican's holdings. The oldest Latin passion follows in the eighth century, three hundred years after the martyrium at Chalcedon was already standing.
suggested_refs: The Greek Passio Sancti Christophori (BHG 309-310c) and its Vatican codices
sources: Wikipedia, 'Saint Christopher'
Zibaldone / Estudios italianos, scholarship on the Passio Sancti Christophori
Orthodox Arts Journal, 'Understanding The Dog-Headed Icon of St. Christopher'

stops.name: Corbie, Ratramnus answers the missionary
stops.date_confidence: attested to c. 863-865, before 865
stops.campa: Rimbert, missionary priest and later Ansgar's successor at Hamburg-Bremen, writes south to Corbie with a practical question: there are dog-headed peoples reported in the far north, and he needs to know whether they may be baptized. Ratramnus answers with a letter on the cynocephali. He weighs their villages, their clothing, their laws, their sense of shame, and the hagiography of Christopher, and rules that they are rational and are to be evangelised. Ratramnus has never seen one. He settles the question out of the fathers and a saint's Life.
suggested_refs: The abbey of Corbie in Picardy, and the Epistola de cynocephalis
sources: Ratramnus of Corbie, Epistola de cynocephalis (c. 863-865)
JSTOR Daily, 'Christopher the Dog-Headed Saint'

stops.name: Speyer, Walter puts the giant into Latin metre
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: At Speyer, Walter completes a Life of Saint Christopher in verse and prose together, the Vita Sancti Christophori versibus et prosa oratione composita. The West now has the giant in Latin metre, three hundred years before Genoa. What the Latin line has already lost, and will not recover, is the tribe: no Marmaritae, no cannibals, no muzzle. The dog's head stays east of the Adriatic, where the icon painters will keep it for another eight hundred years against every prohibition issued.
suggested_refs: The cathedral school of Speyer under bishop Balderich
sources: Wikipedia, 'Saint Christopher'

stops.name: Constantinople, the Synaxarion says fearsome and not dog
stops.date_confidence: 10th century; the Synaxarion of Constantinople is a compilation and no single year applies
stops.campa: The Synaxarion of the Great Church, the calendar with commentary kept in the capital, comes to the ninth of May and describes the martyr as wild and fearsome to look at. It does not say dog. That phrase is the whole warrant the later painters have. Within a few centuries the fearsome look has hardened into a snout, teeth and a pricked ear, panel after panel. The etymological tangle runs the other way as well, Greek kunokephalos giving Latin canineus, misread afterwards as Cananeus, the Canaanite.
suggested_refs: The Synaxarion of Constantinople, entry for 9 May
sources: John Sanidopoulos, 'The Depiction of Saint Christopher with the Head of a Dog' (2018)
Wikipedia, 'Saint Christopher' (on the canineus/Cananeus transmission)

stops.name: Goreme, the beardless soldier in the tufa
stops.date_confidence: 11th century, per the survey of Cappadocian rock churches; no closer dating given
stops.campa: In the rock churches cut into the tufa of Cappadocia, Christopher is painted young, beardless and armed, a soldier martyr among soldier martyrs, hard to tell from George or Theodore. There is no dog in him and no child on his shoulder. These are among the earliest surviving pictures of the saint anywhere. The Eastern church of the eleventh century had the dog-headed Passion in its libraries, and on these walls it painted a man in armour with a human face.
suggested_refs: The rock-cut churches of the Goreme valley, Cappadocia
sources: John Sanidopoulos, 'The Depiction of Saint Christopher with the Head of a Dog' (2018)

stops.name: Karakallou, Mount Athos: the second skull
stops.date_confidence: the monastery is founded by the monk Karakalas and stands by 1018; no date is given anywhere for the relic's arrival
stops.campa: Karakallou, eleventh in the Athonite hierarchy, founded by the monk Karakalas and standing by 1018, keeps in its treasury a skull it venerates as Christopher's, alongside a skull of Bartholomew and a fragment of the True Cross. Rab, in the Adriatic, keeps a skull of Christopher too, in a gold-plated reliquary, and has kept it since the eleventh century. Neither house mentions the other. A saint with one head has two, in treasuries seven hundred miles apart, and the arithmetic has never troubled either.
suggested_refs: The treasury of Karakallou Monastery, Mount Athos
sources: Monastiriaka, 'Holy Monastery of Karakallou'
Athos Forum, 'Karakallou Monastery'

stops.name: Docheiariou, Mount Athos: the child arrives on the shoulder
stops.date_confidence: Palaiologan era, 13th-15th century; the survey names Athos broadly and Docheiariou stands as a representative Athonite pin, not a located fresco
stops.campa: On the Holy Mountain, through the Palaiologan centuries, he is still the beardless soldier, sometimes with the martyr's cross, sometimes now with a child riding his shoulder. Patmos keeps the same figure, and so does the painting of the empire's furthest edges. The child has crossed from the Latin West into Greek painting and the river has not crossed with him. The painters here take the shoulder and the burden, and leave the ford on the far side of the Adriatic with the giant who worked it.
suggested_refs: Docheiariou Monastery and the Athonite Palaiologan programmes; the Monastery of St John the Theologian, Patmos
sources: John Sanidopoulos, 'The Depiction of Saint Christopher with the Head of a Dog' (2018)
Orthodox Arts Journal, 'Understanding The Dog-Headed Icon of St. Christopher'

stops.name: Tarnovo, the two Christophers on one wall
stops.date_confidence: the Palaiologan layer is 13th-15th century; the bearded Christ-bearing figure at the Church of the Apostles Peter and Paul is dated to the end of the 15th century, post-Byzantine
stops.campa: In the old capital of the Second Bulgarian Empire, in the church of the Apostles Peter and Paul, Christopher appears twice over. In the Palaiologan layer he is the young beardless soldier of Athos and Patmos. In a later layer, painted at the end of the fifteenth century, he is bearded and carries the infant Christ on his shoulder, and by then the empire that commissioned the first layer no longer exists. The two figures are commonly run together as one image; they are two phases, a century and a conquest apart.
suggested_refs: The Church of the Holy Apostles Peter and Paul, Veliko Tarnovo
sources: John Sanidopoulos, 'The Depiction of Saint Christopher with the Head of a Dog' (2018)

segments.name: The Relic Coast and the Golden Legend

stops.name: Rab, the skull on the town wall
stops.date_confidence: the siege and the 9 May commemoration are local tradition from the 11th century; the reliquary itself is dated to the 11th century on stylistic grounds
stops.campa: An Italo-Norman fleet lays siege to Rab. Bishop Raduald carries the reliquary out onto the town wall and turns the skull of Saint Christopher toward the attackers, and the arrows loosed at the wall turn in the air and go back into the men who shot them. The town holds. Rab takes him for patron, builds three centuries of civic identity on the relic, and keeps the ninth of May as the Dies Victoriae. The gold-plated reliquary is eleventh-century work; the chain of custody back to Constantinople is tradition and nothing else.
suggested_refs: The reliquary of the skull of St Christopher, Museum of Sacred Art at St Justine's church, Rab
sources: Brepols / Ikon journal, 'The Cult of Saint Christopher in the Diocese of Rab: Relic, Hagiography and Iconography'
kristofor.hr
rab-visit.com

stops.name: Genoa, the Legenda Aurea fixes the ferryman
stops.date_confidence: attested by traditional dating of the compilation, c. 1260
stops.campa: Jacobus da Voragine, Dominican and later archbishop of this city, compiles the Legenda Aurea, and the chapter he gives Christopher is the ferryman entire: the giant Reprobus twelve cubits high, the king, the devil, the hermit, the river, the child, the staff in flower. There is no tribe of dog-headed cannibals anywhere in it. Caxton prints it in English in 1483 and the ferryman becomes the only Christopher the West can remember. Margaret of Antioch and Catherine of Alexandria travel chapters away in the same book, and in this atlas.
suggested_refs: The Dominican convent of Genoa, where the Legenda Sanctorum was compiled
sources: Jacobus de Voragine, Legenda Aurea
EBSCO Research Starters, 'Saint Christopher'

stops.name: Vercelli, the tooth bigger than a fist
stops.date_confidence: late medieval; no year is given for the enshrinement, and the debunking is dated only to the late 18th century
stops.campa: The Humiliati of San Cristoforo enshrine a molar in silver and gold: the tooth of the giant, the proof of the size of him. Juan Luis Vives sees it and calls it a molar tooth bigger than a fist. The friars are suppressed in 1571 and the Barnabites carry the veneration on to the end of the eighteenth century, when a naturalist looks at the object and says hippopotamus. It comes off the altar and public veneration of it is forbidden. The relic that best proved him a giant proved instead that comparative anatomy had arrived.
suggested_refs: The church of San Cristoforo, Vercelli, and its lost tooth reliquary
sources: British Dental Journal (2019), 'The gigantic tooth of St. Christopher'

stops.name: Sibenik, the leg out of Constantinople
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1484 by the cathedral's own tradition and altar inscription
stops.campa: A leg comes from Constantinople by way of Corfu, intended for Korcula and landing here instead: the foot, the shin and the femur of St Christopher the Martyr, as the silver plaque on the altar reads. The cathedral is dedicated to St James and St Christopher together. Rab, ninety miles up the same coast, holds his skull and traces it to Constantinople as well. Neither church's account of its own relic mentions the other's, and no source explains how one body supplied both ends of it.
suggested_refs: The Cathedral of St James and St Christopher, Sibenik, and its relic altar
sources: Wikipedia, 'Saint Christopher'
Cathedral of St James, Sibenik (UNESCO listing)

segments.name: The Fourteen Helpers and the Giant at the Door

stops.name: Regensburg, the Fourteen Holy Helpers against the plague
stops.date_confidence: the cult of the Fourteen forms in Franconia and the Rhineland around the Black Death; no founding decree exists and the date is conventional
stops.campa: Plague comes up the Danube, and the invocation of fourteen saints together as one company takes hold in Franconia and the Rhineland. Barbara against sudden death, Margaret against the pains of birth, Catherine for the dying, Giles for the confession nobody dares make, Christopher against plague itself and against dying unshriven on the road. Four of them already travel in this atlas. He is the fifth, and the tallest. The company is fixed by usage and not by decree: no bull creates it and none is needed.
suggested_refs: Regensburg and the Franconian cult of the Vierzehn Nothelfer
sources: saint_barbara.journey.json, stop 'Regensburg, the Fourteen Holy Helpers gathered against the plague'
QUEUE.md, entry 'Los Catorce Santos Ayudantes'

stops.name: Norton Priory, eleven feet of stone against sudden death
stops.date_confidence: carved near the end of the 14th century; no year attested
stops.campa: In the Augustinian priory at Runcorn a Christopher is carved three and a third metres high in stone, the largest medieval statue of him left in Britain. The height is the doctrine. A traveller who saw an image of Christopher in the morning was held safe from sudden death for that day, so the images were made big enough to be read from the road and set where the road could see them: on a church wall opposite the door, at the head of a bridge, over the gate. The priory is dissolved; the giant outlasts the house that carved him.
suggested_refs: The statue of St Christopher, Norton Priory Museum, Runcorn, Cheshire
sources: Wikipedia, 'Statue of St Christopher, Norton Priory'

stops.name: Paris, the colossus inside the west door of Notre-Dame
stops.date_confidence: commission attested to 1413; the statue is recorded as knocked down in 1785
stops.campa: Antoine des Essarts, chamberlain to Charles VI, pays for a Christopher some twenty-eight feet high to stand inside the west door of Notre-Dame, where everyone entering the cathedral passes beneath him. He stands there three hundred and seventy-two years. In 1785 the chapter has him taken down to let more light into the nave. Popular accounts afterwards hand the destruction to the revolutionary Cult of Reason; the chapter's own order is four years earlier than the Revolution and is about daylight.
suggested_refs: The lost colossal St Christopher of Notre-Dame de Paris, west end, north side
sources: Wikidata, 'colossal statue of Saint Christopher'
Penelope.uchicago.edu, 'St. Christopher, Notre Dame de Paris'

stops.name: Buxheim, the first dated print in Europe
stops.date_confidence: attested by the date cut into the block itself
stops.campa: In the Carthusian house at Buxheim in Swabia a woodblock is cut and inked: Christopher in the water with the child on his shoulder, the hermit with his lantern on the bank, and a date in the margin. It is the earliest dated European print. The first image printing carries out into the world is the giant who carries. Pilgrims paste the sheet inside chest lids and on the walls of rooms, where looking at it each morning does the work the stone giants at the church doors were doing.
suggested_refs: The Buxheim St Christopher woodcut of 1423, John Rylands Library, Manchester
sources: Wikipedia, 'Saint Christopher'

stops.name: Vierzehnheiligen, the shepherd counts fourteen children
stops.date_confidence: attested date of the second vision in the Langheim tradition
stops.campa: In a field belonging to the Cistercians of Langheim, a shepherd named Hermann Leicht sees a child sitting in the grass, and later the child again with two candles beside it, and later still fourteen children who tell him that they are the fourteen helpers and that they want a chapel built here. Giles is admitted to that company in this atlas, and Barbara, and Catherine, and Margaret. Christopher stands among the same fourteen, though the shepherd's vision as it is recorded does not count them off by name.
suggested_refs: The Basilica of Vierzehnheiligen, above the Main near Bad Staffelstein
sources: giles.journey.json, stop 'Vierzehnheiligen, among the Fourteen Holy Helpers'
saint_barbara.journey.json

stops.name: Havana, the first Mass under the ceiba
stops.date_confidence: traditional only: the municipal records to 1550 were burned by Jacques de Sores, so the exact founding day is unrecoverable
stops.campa: On the western side of the bay, under a ceiba tree, the settlers hear the first Mass and hold the first meeting of the council, and the town takes the name San Cristobal de La Habana. It is the third siting; an earlier attempt on the south coast near Batabano failed. He is the patron of travellers, sailors and muleteers, which is the entire business of the place. The date is traditional: Jacques de Sores burns the municipal records to 1550, and after that no document can confirm the day.
suggested_refs: El Templete, Plaza de Armas, Havana, on the site of the ceiba and the first Mass
sources: La Habana (gob.cu), 'Por que la capital de Cuba se llamo San Cristobal de La Habana?'
CiberCuba, 'Fundacion de la Villa de San Cristobal de La Habana'

stops.name: San Cristobal de las Casas, the highland town takes the name
stops.date_confidence: founded 1528 as Villa Real de Chiapa; the renaming is drawn from general colonial record rather than a document read in this pass
stops.campa: In the highlands of Chiapas the Spanish found Villa Real de Chiapa, which becomes Ciudad Real and then, under the same patron as Havana, San Cristobal, with de las Casas added afterwards for the Dominican bishop who fought the encomienda from its cathedral. The crown gives the same name to town after town across the Americas, wherever a road runs and a river has to be crossed. The founding date is broadly rather than precisely attested, and no single source was fetched for the renaming.
suggested_refs: San Cristobal de las Casas, Chiapas, and its cathedral of the Dominican mission
sources: General colonial-history record of the founding and renaming of San Cristobal de las Casas

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the barrio on the third hill
stops.date_confidence: the barrio's name is 19th-century; no source consulted in this pass dates the naming, and the year is a placeholder for the parish era
stops.campa: A barrio south-west of the Plaza de Mayo takes his name and keeps it, and on its streets stands the third-highest natural ground in the city, which in a city this flat counts as a hill by courtesy. Emin Arslan, consul and traveller, works this same Buenos Aires in the atlas. The barrio's connection to the saint is nominal: no relic, no legend, no crossing, only the name of the traveller's patron laid over a grid of blocks by people who had themselves just arrived off ships.
suggested_refs: The barrio of San Cristobal, Buenos Aires
sources: emin_arslan.journey.json (shared Buenos Aires pin)

segments.name: The Calendars Divide, the Medals Do Not

stops.name: Rome, the Tridentine calendar enters the feast
stops.date_confidence: mid-16th century; the sources give the period of the reformed Roman calendar rather than a year
stops.campa: The reformed Roman calendar of the Tridentine period enters his feast on the twenty-fifth of July. He has been kept in the churches for eleven hundred years by then and is only now written into the universal calendar of the Latin rite. In 1954 the commemoration is extended to all Masses of the day, the high-water mark of his official standing. That gap of eleven centuries between the living cult and the calendar entry is the entire argument the twentieth century will use to take him out again.
suggested_refs: The Roman Tridentine calendar and the feast of 25 July
sources: Wikipedia, 'Saint Christopher'

stops.name: Moscow, the Synod bans the dog's head
stops.date_confidence: attested to the 1722 Synod; a separate 18th-century Moscow proscription cited elsewhere without a year is almost certainly this same act
stops.campa: The Holy Synod bans the dog-headed icon and orders him painted as a man. The Old Believers, outside the Synod's discipline, go on painting the muzzle. Panels survive from the seventeenth century with an unmistakable canine snout set on a bearded warrior's shoulders, and the type does not die: the ban on the Old Believers' practice is lifted in 1971, two hundred and forty-nine years after it was imposed. In the surviving Greek panels the literal dog's head is no older than the Ottoman period, which makes the image younger than the prohibition assumes.
suggested_refs: The Most Holy Synod of the Russian Church and the icon-painting regulations of 1722
sources: Wikipedia, 'Saint Christopher'
Orthodox Arts Journal, 'Understanding The Dog-Headed Icon of St. Christopher'
John Sanidopoulos, 'The Depiction of Saint Christopher with the Head of a Dog'

stops.name: Prague, the crossing guarded by the crossing
stops.date_confidence: 19th century; the source gives the century and the sculptor, Emanuel Max, but no year
stops.campa: On the south side of the Charles Bridge, Emanuel Max sets a Christopher among the baroque company of saints, the child on his shoulder above the Vltava. The bridge is a crossing, and the crossing is guarded by the man who was one. The statue is nineteenth-century work standing inside a seventeenth-century programme. The Vltava runs below, and the passengers on the boats look up at him from the water, which is the old bargain of the Buxheim sheet: see Christopher in the morning and travel safe.
suggested_refs: The statue of St Christopher by Emanuel Max, Charles Bridge, Prague
sources: Wikipedia, 'Statue of Saint Christopher, Charles Bridge'

stops.name: Vatican City, struck from the calendar
stops.date_confidence: attested: promulgated 1969, in force from 1970
stops.campa: The revision of the General Roman Calendar removes his feast from the universal calendar and leaves it to local and regional calendars, on the grounds that no historically verifiable Passion stands under the legend and the feast entered the calendar only in the sixteenth century. The twenty-fifth of July goes to St James. He is not decanonized, and his name stays in the Roman Martyrology, which almost nobody reads. What the world hears is that the Church has declared him a myth, and not one dashboard medal comes down.
suggested_refs: Calendarium Romanum (1969) and the motu proprio Mysterii Paschalis
sources: General Roman Calendar of 1969
Catholic Answers, 'Did the Church declare that St. Christopher is a myth?'
The Automobile and American Life, 'Driving With A St. Christopher Medal on the Dashboard'

stops.name: Rab, the crossbowmen and the Rabska Fjera
stops.date_confidence: attested as current practice
stops.campa: The town keeps the ninth of May for the arrows that turned, and in late July it keeps the Rabska Fjera: three days for St James, St Anne and St Christopher together, with the crossbowmen shooting in the old square. The skull sits in the museum at St Justine's now, rather than on the wall over the harbour. Rome no longer requires the feast anywhere. Nine hundred and fifty years after the siege the arrows are aimed at targets, and the giant is still the reason for the date.
suggested_refs: The Rabska Fjera and the crossbowmen's games, Rab, 25-27 July
